## Introduction

This article is about where time and memory go when you run a dplyr pipeline
through cuplyr, and when to choose eager or lazy execution. It has numbers from
one machine, a list of cases where the GPU loses to plain dplyr, and advice
that follows from both. `vignette("query-optimization", package = "cuplyr")`
explains what the optimizer passes do. This one measures what they buy.

The short version: lazy is the better choice for pipelines, but not because it
is faster. When GPU memory is clean it is slower at every table size measured:
about 1 ms per pipeline up to 1e6 rows, 2.4 ms at 1e7 and 3 ms at 5e7. What it
gives you is that every intermediate column is freed when the pipeline
finishes, so it stays safe on big tables and in loops. In a loop an eager
pipeline's leftovers pile up, and once they fill the card cuplyr's
out-of-memory handler has to run. That made eager 3 to 7 times slower than lazy
in the measurements below. Until the card is full eager stays faster: in a
separate run at 2.5e7 rows, five back-to-back eager calls left about 4 GB
behind and still took 9.4 ms each, against 12 ms lazy.

```{r setup}
library(cuplyr)
library(dplyr)
```

## How a cuplyr call runs

Each verb call does some work in R (check the arguments, work out the new
schema) and then, in eager mode, some work on the GPU. At 1e3 rows the GPU part
is tiny and the R part dominates. A profile of one eager verb at 1e3 rows put
about 90% of the time on the R side. That fixed cost is the per-call floor, and
it is why most single verbs on small tables are not faster than dplyr
(`arrange()` is).

The two modes differ in when the GPU work happens.

- **Eager.** Each verb runs at once and returns a GPU table. Every
  intermediate table stays allocated until R's garbage collector drops it.
- **Lazy.** Each verb checks its arguments, works out the new schema and
  records a node in a plan, without touching the GPU. `compute()` optimizes the
  plan, runs it, and keeps the result on the GPU. `collect()` does the same and
  then copies the result to R. The intermediates are freed when the call
  returns.

You choose the mode per table with `tbl_gpu(df, lazy = TRUE)`, or for every
table created afterwards with `options(cuplyr.exec_mode = "lazy")`.
`show_query()` prints the pending steps of a lazy table. `explain()` prints them
next to the plan the optimizer will actually run:

```{r explain, eval = FALSE}
lazy <- tbl_gpu(mtcars, lazy = TRUE) |>
  filter(mpg > 20) |>
  mutate(kpl = mpg * 0.425, hp2 = hp * 2) |>
  select(cyl, kpl)

explain(lazy)
#> Pending operations:
#> ast_select [2 cols]
#> | ast_mutate [2 expressions]
#> | | ast_filter [1 predicates]
#> | | | ast_source [11 cols]
#>
#> AST depth: 4
#> Node count: 4
#>
#> Optimized plan:
#> ast_select [2 cols]
#> | ast_mutate [1 expressions]
#> | | ast_select [2 cols]
#> | | | ast_filter [1 predicates]
#> | | | | ast_source [11 cols]
```

```{r explain-run, echo = FALSE}
# The output above is pasted so a default build shows it. A build with GPU
# evaluation runs the same code and fails if explain() no longer prints it.
lazy <- tbl_gpu(mtcars, lazy = TRUE) |>
  filter(mpg > 20) |>
  mutate(kpl = mpg * 0.425, hp2 = hp * 2) |>
  select(cyl, kpl)
stopifnot(identical(
  trimws(capture.output(explain(lazy))),
  c("Pending operations:",
    "ast_select [2 cols]",
    "| ast_mutate [2 expressions]",
    "| | ast_filter [1 predicates]",
    "| | | ast_source [11 cols]",
    "",
    "AST depth: 4",
    "Node count: 4",
    "",
    "Optimized plan:",
    "ast_select [2 cols]",
    "| ast_mutate [1 expressions]",
    "| | ast_select [2 cols]",
    "| | | ast_filter [1 predicates]",
    "| | | | ast_source [11 cols]")
))
```

In the optimized plan the mutate has one expression instead of two, because
nothing uses `hp2`, and a select keeps only the 2 needed columns before the
mutate. Nothing has run on the GPU yet. `collect(lazy)` runs the plan.

The optimizer runs five passes when `compute()` or `collect()` is called:

- **Projection pruning** inserts a select that keeps only the columns the later
  steps need (the inner select in the plan above).
- **Mutate fusion** merges consecutive `mutate()` calls into one node, so they
  run as one step. It keeps the expressions in the order you wrote them, and
  it does not merge when the result would have more than 8 expressions or
  when the later `mutate()` reads more than 4 columns the earlier one creates.
- **Dead-column pruning** drops mutate outputs that nothing later uses (`hp2`
  above).
- **Filter pushdown** usually moves a filter below a mutate when the filter
  does not read a column that mutate computes, so the mutate sees fewer rows.
  It also moves filters below a `select()` that keeps their columns, and into
  the inputs of some joins. Whether a join allows it depends on its type and on
  its `relationship`, `multiple` and `unmatched` arguments; `explain()` shows
  where each filter ended up.
- **Filter reordering** usually merges consecutive `filter()` calls into one
  filter node, which builds one row mask and selects the rows once. It also
  sorts the merged predicates so the cheaper ones (estimated from the size of
  each expression) come first. Eager runs each `filter()` call on its own and
  allocates the filtered table in between.

A single `filter()` call with several predicates is already one filter node in
both modes: its predicates are combined with `&` into one expression. The
optimizer leaves their order alone unless it merges the call with another
filter. Some verbs, such as `arrange()` and
`summarise()`, are barriers: the passes run on each side of them but not
across.
`vignette("query-optimization", package = "cuplyr")` has the details.

## Measurements

Everything below is a static table. Nothing in this vignette is timed when it is
built. The code that produced the numbers is at the end.

- Date and code: 2026-10-23, cuplyr 0.1.1.9000 at commit b39a8f1.
- Hardware and software: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5070 (12 GB), driver 615.78.08,
  R 4.6.1, dplyr 1.2.1. Memory resource `async` (the default).
- Method: data already on the GPU (uploads are not in the pipeline timings),
  warm, median of 15 samples (9 at 5e7 rows). Each sample timed a batch of
  calls fenced with `gpu_sync()`. The batch size came from one timed call and
  aimed at 30 ms, but the timer has 1 ms resolution, so batches of
  sub-millisecond calls ran anywhere from 4 to 118 ms. Calls slower than 30 ms
  ran one per batch. R's `gc()` ran, untimed, before every batch. Each number is
  the median of three fresh R processes, and the three runs differed by about
  10% at most (the 0.23 ms `arrange()` call) and by under 5% for the
  pipelines.

### A five-verb pipeline

```r
filter(x > 0.1) |> mutate(z = x * y + w) |> group_by(g) |>
  summarise(m = mean(z), n = n()) |> arrange(desc(m)) |> collect()
```

The table has an integer `g` with 100 groups and double columns `x`, `y` and
`w`. The dplyr column runs the same pipeline on a tibble. "Held" is how much
GPU memory the call leaves allocated until R's next `gc()`, measured as the
growth of `gpu_memory_state()$pool_used_bytes` across one call whose result is
collected.

| rows | eager ms | lazy ms | dplyr ms | eager held MB | lazy held MB |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1e3 | 3.10 | 4.14 | 3.50 | 0.03 | 0 |
| 1e6 | 3.25 | 4.25 | 24.5 | 32 | 0 |
| 1e7 | 4.83 | 7.20 | 211 | 324 | 0 |
| 5e7 | 17.5 | 20.5 | not run | 1620 | 0 |
| 5e7, 5 calls back to back, no `gc()` | 68.2 | 20.2 | not run | | |

The last row is what a loop or a script does: it runs the pipeline five times
without a `gc()` in between and reports the mean time per call. It shows the
cautious end of a range. The eager figure depends on what the memory pool already
holds. In two later runs of the same five-call loop it was 145 and 155 ms per
call, against 22 and 24 ms for lazy.

### One eager verb at 1e3 rows (the per-call floor)

No `collect()`. The result stays on the GPU.

| verb | cuplyr ms | dplyr ms |
|---|---|---|
| filter | 0.73 | 0.35 |
| mutate | 0.83 | 0.40 |
| select | 0.58 | 0.42 |
| arrange | 0.23 | 0.68 |
| grouped summarise | 0.81 | 0.77 |

### Transfers (4 columns)

| rows | `tbl_gpu()` upload ms | `collect()` of all rows ms |
|---|---|---|
| 1e3 | 0.14 | 0.12 |
| 1e6 | 6.60 | 6.00 |
| 1e7 | 68.0 | 54.0 |

### A case built for the optimizer

A 21-column table (`g` plus `x1` to `x20`), one query that computes columns it
later drops and filters after the mutate:

```r
mutate(a = x1 * 2, b = x2 * x3, c = x4 + x5) |> filter(x1 > 0.9) |>
  select(g, a) |> collect()
```

`explain()` shows the optimizer reading 2 of the 21 columns at the source,
running the filter below the mutate, and dropping `b` and `c`.

| rows | eager ms | lazy ms | dplyr ms | eager held MB | lazy held MB |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1e6 | 3.37 | 4.14 | 22.0 | 43 | 0 |
| 1e7 | 7.00 | 7.20 | 182 | 428 | 0 |

### Reading the table

- With clean GPU memory, lazy is slower than eager at every size measured: by
  1.0 ms at 1e3 and 1e6 rows, 2.4 ms at 1e7 and 3.0 ms at 5e7. At 1e7 rows that
  is 49% longer (7.20 against 4.83 ms), at 5e7 rows 17% (20.5 against 17.5 ms).
  The gap does not close on big tables. In milliseconds it grows with the row
  count, but as a share of the run time it does not.
- Where the first millisecond goes: recording the five-verb plan costs about as
  much R time as running the whole eager pipeline, because each lazy verb still
  checks its arguments and works out the schema (2.7 against 3.0 ms at 1e3 rows
  in the follow-up run below). Then `collect()` optimizes and lowers the plan,
  about 1 ms more (1.2 ms at 1e3 rows). Recording time does not depend on the
  row count, so that is not what grows with it.
- Why the gap grows: GPU calls return before the kernels finish, so an eager
  pipeline runs one verb's GPU work while R prepares the next verb. Lazy records
  the whole plan before any GPU work starts and loses that overlap. A separate
  follow-up run at 1e7 rows (not part of the table above) shows it: eager took
  4.67 ms, eager with a `gpu_sync()` after every verb 6.2 ms, lazy 7.0 ms. In
  that run recording the lazy plan took 2.6 ms and `collect()` of the recorded
  plan 4.25 ms. At 1e3 rows the `gpu_sync()` after every verb added only 0.1 ms
  (3.0 to 3.1 ms), because there is little GPU work to overlap.
- The optimizer did not make lazy faster than eager in the case built for it:
  4.14 against 3.37 ms at 1e6 rows and 7.20 against 7.00 ms at 1e7. At these
  sizes there is too little GPU work for the skipped work to pay back lazy's
  extra R-side cost and lost overlap. Lazy still wins on memory there, as in
  every case: it held nothing, eager held 428 MB.
- Memory is the reason to prefer lazy. Here an eager pipeline leaves about 32
  bytes per row behind until R's next `gc()`: 324 MB at 1e7 rows, 1620 MB at
  5e7. Run it again before the `gc()` and the memory pool keeps growing. In a
  traced run of the five-call loop it went from 5.4 to 11.6 GB on a 12 GB card,
  and then cuplyr's out-of-memory handler ran `gc()` and `gpu_gc()` and retried
  the step. This is what happens in the back-to-back row: 68.2 ms against
  20.2 ms, lazy 3.4 times faster. The two later runs gave 6.6 and 6.7 times.
- Before the card fills, eager stays faster. In a separate run at 2.5e7 rows
  (not part of the tables), five back-to-back eager calls left about 4 GB
  behind and took 9.4 ms each, against 12 ms lazy.
- Against dplyr on a tibble at 1e3 rows, eager is about even (3.10 against
  3.50 ms) and lazy is about 0.6 ms slower (4.14 ms). At 1e6 rows cuplyr is 5.8
  to 7.5 times faster, and at 1e7 rows 29 to 44 times.

## Where the GPU loses

- **Tiny tables.** At 1e3 rows a single cuplyr call takes 0.23 to 0.83 ms,
  almost all of it R-side work. Every single verb above is slower than dplyr
  except `arrange()`, and the grouped `summarise()` is close to a tie. A whole
  pipeline at that size is about even with dplyr eager (3.10 against 3.50 ms)
  and about 0.6 ms slower lazy (4.14 ms).
- **Transfers.** Moving data costs more than the compute. Uploading 1e7 rows
  takes 68 ms and collecting them 54 ms, against 4.83 ms for the eager
  pipeline. If you upload, run one cheap verb and collect, the GPU loses.
- **CPU fallbacks.** Some expressions have no GPU translation, and cuplyr
  evaluates them in R instead, copying data across. This is silent by default.
  Set `options(cuplyr.fallback = "warn")` to be told when it happens, or
  `"error"` to forbid it.

## Practical advice

- Upload once and keep the data on the GPU between steps. Collect once, at the
  end of the pipeline.
- Use lazy for pipelines, most of all on big tables and in loops, where not
  holding intermediates matters. Do not expect it to be faster: with clean GPU
  memory it was slower at every size measured. It wins when an eager pipeline's
  leftovers pile up.
- Use eager for interactive exploration and single calls where you want each
  result at once.
- To branch from a shared prefix, `compute()` it once and build the branches
  from the result. It keeps the table on the GPU.
- After dropping a large eager result, `gc()` frees it back to cuplyr's memory
  pool, where the next calls reuse it. `gpu_gc()` does that too and then returns
  the pool's unused memory to the card, so other processes can use it. It takes
  about a second and the next calls have to grow the pool again, so use it when
  you need the memory elsewhere, not inside a loop.
  `vignette("memory", package = "cuplyr")` covers the memory resources and when
  memory is freed.
- Fence GPU timings with `gpu_sync()`. GPU calls return before the kernels
  finish, so a timer without it may stop the clock before the GPU work is
  done.
- Check `explain()` when a lazy pipeline is slower than you expect. See
  `vignette("query-optimization", package = "cuplyr")` for the passes.

## Reproduce

This is a trimmed copy of the script behind the tables, covering the pipeline
timings and the memory column. It is not run when the vignette is built. Run it
in a fresh session on an idle GPU. It sizes each batch from one timed call
that the 1 ms timer resolution rounds, so batches of sub-millisecond calls can
run well under or over the 30 ms it aims for.

```{r reproduce, eval = FALSE}
library(cuplyr)
library(dplyr)
set.seed(1)

# Median ms per call. A sample is a batch of calls fenced with gpu_sync();
# gc() runs untimed before every batch.
per_call <- function(fn, samples = 15, warmup = 3, target = 0.03) {
  for (i in seq_len(warmup)) fn()
  gpu_sync(); gc(verbose = FALSE)
  t0 <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]; fn(); gpu_sync()
  one <- max(proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t0, 1e-4)
  reps <- max(1L, min(500L, as.integer(ceiling(target / one))))
  t <- vapply(seq_len(samples), function(i) {
    gc(verbose = FALSE)
    t0 <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
    for (j in seq_len(reps)) fn()
    gpu_sync()
    (proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t0) / reps
  }, numeric(1))
  1e3 * median(t)
}

# GPU memory one call leaves allocated until R's next gc(), in MB.
held_mb <- function(fn) {
  gc(verbose = FALSE); gc(verbose = FALSE); gpu_sync()
  u0 <- gpu_memory_state()$pool_used_bytes
  r <- fn(); gpu_sync()
  u1 <- gpu_memory_state()$pool_used_bytes
  rm(r)
  (u1 - u0) / 1e6
}

pipeline <- function(d) {
  d |>
    filter(x > 0.1) |>
    mutate(z = x * y + w) |>
    group_by(g) |>
    summarise(m = mean(z), n = n()) |>
    arrange(desc(m))
}

n <- 1e6
df <- data.frame(g = sample.int(100L, n, TRUE), x = runif(n), y = runif(n),
                 w = rnorm(n))
tb <- tibble::as_tibble(df)
eg <- tbl_gpu(df, lazy = FALSE)
lz <- tbl_gpu(df, lazy = TRUE)

c(eager = per_call(function() collect(pipeline(eg))),
  lazy  = per_call(function() collect(pipeline(lz))),
  dplyr = per_call(function() pipeline(tb)))
c(eager = held_mb(function() collect(pipeline(eg))),
  lazy  = held_mb(function() collect(pipeline(lz))))
```
